utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Wednesday, the 30th of January, 2008. Good morning, Witness. Good morning, Ms. Dahl. Good morning, Mr. Seselj, and my morning greetings to all the people helping us. Before I give the floor to Ms. Dahl for her to proceed with the examination-in-chief, I'd like to turn to Mr. Seselj on two points. The first one has to do with the objection he has raised. The second has to do with the tone or volume of his voice. First of all the objections. As you know, Mr. Seselj, objections are allowed, especially so in common law trials. Why so? Because as a rule in common law countries, you have a jury that expresses guilt or innocence. The Judge is only there as an umpire, as an arbiter. It is the jury that decides on the qualification of an offence to see whether an accused is guilty or not, and these are juries made up of citizens. Therefore, one should not use or influence their point of view or feelings through biased questions. Therefore, when there are leading questions, parties can raise objections. But the difference there is between such common law countries and this International Tribunal is that this International Tribunal is made up of professional Judges. You have a Bench of three Judges who each are very experienced in international trials. They have sat in several trials already. Therefore, if for some extraordinary reason there was a leading question that was put, the Judges would immediately realise that and they would automatically reassess the scope of the answer taking into account the leading aspect of the question. Therefore, if there were to be a leading question, trust the Judges. They will see it is a leading question. In this way, we can save time. More often than not, and this is my experience that shows it, when there is a leading question it means that the one putting the question is trying to save time. He is trying to do well. He does not want to manipulate Judges. More often than not the main reason being that one wants to proceed swiftly, thereby sometimes having to put leading questions. This has to do with objections. If you have a basic objection to raise, do so, but when it deals to borderline questions, do not, please, intervene too often. And everything I'm telling you today should not be understood as a reproach, criticism. It's more of an advice so that the trial proceedings can unfold as smoothly as possible for everybody's sake. Second point, the tone or volume of your voice. You have said so yourself, you are very loud. That's your past, your childhood. You said so yourself, the fact that you were a lecturer, a professor, a university professor, and when you teach you have to speak to students, and when you have many of them you have to raise the volume of your voice. And you were also a major political figure so used to holding speeches where voice is a support to those who are supposed to hear you. But this is a small courtroom. We're not far from one another. We're just a few metres away from each other so we can hear each other. So it might be good if you could lower your voice and have less decibels. I watched a few videos disclosed by the Prosecution in their many submissions when you give interviews to journalists; you did not raise your voice. So I wondered, When he speaks to a journalist he speaks calmly. Why can't he do the same in the courtroom? So try to speak more softly. That would be a plus for everybody. Let me give you an example. Yesterday, for instance, you spoke about two events in particular. As to the first one, you challenged the facts or the authenticity of a document. You said that the Communists had forged this directive of December 1941 - this is what I'm quoting from memory - and you said that in a very loud voice. And at the very end of the hearing Ms. Dahl gave us this document I'm showing you, and equally you intervened and in a very loud voice you asked where the document came from. You used the same tone for these two events. Of course, one was important. It is the issue of whether a document is a fake or not. The other one was not so important, because this was about the provenance of this document. By using the same volume or tone of voice for the essential and what is not essential, it might prove difficult for Judges to sort the grain from the chaff. For instance, when somebody speaks calmly and then all of a sudden raises their voice one can wonder if something important is happening. But when the tone is always loud, the listener may find it very difficult to see what is essential and what is not essential. This is what I wanted to tell you for us to try and work as best as we can so that the atmosphere is the best possible in the courtroom and also so that we can really go to the crux of the matter, to the merits of the case and not just issues of procedural nature which are a waste of time. I've said that on several occasions. The trial -- or the judgement will not be about the procedure but about the merits of the case. That is what is important to me, to all of us, and should be important to all of us. So let's go to the substance, and let's try to avoid wasting time on procedural issues. Now, regarding your voice, do your best. This is what I wanted to tell you. I don't know whether you wanted to say something, Mr. Seselj. Otherwise, we can proceed with the examination-in-chief. Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, first of all, I have three points to make. First of all, I think that you should take into account all my procedural objections and all the objections of Mrs. Dahl in the course of the proceedings so far. This is only the third witness so far, and you will see that my objections were far more appropriate than those of Mrs. Dahl. My interventions were mostly justified. It happened for the first time yesterday that you told me on two occasions that they were not justified, whereas in most cases Mrs. Dahl's objections are not appropriate. Secondly, leading questions are not allowed in common law or continental law, and they're not allowed in this Tribunal either, and they were not permitted in any cases tried so far. The fact that Defence lawyers are afraid of opposing the Prosecution, and this is a major issue which will go down in the history of world jurisdiction in a negative sense. As for the tone of voice, it is impossible to control a person's individuality. I am doing my very best now to keep my voice down, but at times I react in the natural way I would in my daily life. You may have watched an interview with a journalist when I spoke very quietly. Maybe I was tired. Maybe it happened when I was sick or after several nights without sleep. You could have had somebody in the courtroom who can't speak properly, who mutters and still you have to listen or you could have someone who speaks very quietly and you can't hear him or somebody who has been operated on and he needs an aid. And this is again can be unpleasant. This is something very specific to each individual. I will say again I shall do my best to keep my voice down, but I am still quite confident that the technical services can find a solution by adjusting the microphones. And a third point which is very important. This witness is not so important for me. He's a member of the Prosecution team. He has been engaged by them for four years and therefore he is biased, but imagine if you were to lecture me this way in front of an ordinary man and then you reduce my authority in front of him. Judge May did this very frequently in Mr. Milosevic's trial. He attacks him in the presence of the witness and then the witness gives himself the liberty to act in an inappropriate manner. I don't think it's fair for me to be lectured in the presence of the witness unless there is real cause during the proceedings. So I will leave aside this witness who is a member of the Prosecution team, but in the future if you have any advice or criticisms of this kind, please do so in the absence of the witness. Of course this is something I cannot prevent you from doing. You are fully entitled to it, but I don't think it's fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Apparently Ms. Dahl used one hour and 34 minutes. This is what I was told by the registrar. You have the floor, Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I want to follow up on the document we gave out yesterday in the Serbian language that you mentioned in -- that your advice to Dr. Seselj. It bears registration number 06198785, and I'd like to have this marked, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be MFI P149.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. The document without a title cannot be identified -- marked for identification unless it has a title, the author, the date, the publication, and place of publication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Dahl, will you tell us where this document comes from? Where does the document come from, Ms. Dahl?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Of course I'd like Mr. Tomic to tell us since it was material that he provided. What I have here is a two-page document. It's an excerpt from an a book by Djuro Stanisavljevic, pages 96 and 97 in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, can you tell me what this excerpt is from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please tell us, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a text by Djuro Stanisavljevic, dealing with the development of the Chetnik Movement in Croatia in 1941 and 1942. It was published in Istorija XX. veka. So this is a compilation of academic work, and it was published in 1962 in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you give the name again, spelling it of this journalist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's an historian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in the English text it says journalist. He's a historian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what is his name because the name was not spelled out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stanisavljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can see the name at the very top in the left corner. Now, what is the title of the publication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see in the -- on the top of the second page. The emergent and -- of the Chetnik Movement in Croatia 1941, 1942.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that Mr. Seselj is satisfied with this answer. A technical question to Mr. Seselj. Yes, Judge, I was going to say that. When was it published? This book was published in 1962, wasn't it? Mr. Seselj, when an MFI number is given, it means that the document is not admitted because some things fail yet. For instance, there's no translation or we don't have this type of information yet. This is what I wanted to tell you, to inform you. The same will apply for you when you present documents. If there is no translation or if there are certain things that fail, that are missing, you will be given an MFI number for the document. Please proceed, Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you rely on this text of the emergence and development of the Chetnik Movement in Croatia, 1941 to 1942, in the preparation of your analysis and report?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is one of the sources I used about the Chetnik Dinaric division inasmuch as there is an analysis and presentation of the political programme drafted in March 1942 by this division in this document. So you have parts of it in these two pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: This -- this book appears in your bibliography, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And if you can look at your footnote 97 of your report. Can you tell me whether this text is the one that you have quoted?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: With regard to the reputation of Chetniks and their combat during World War II, can you advise the Chamber what that reputation was and whether it was a matter of common knowledge in society?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When massacres were committed, violent acts were committed and harm was done to individuals. This being said, you must remember this is also quite a pitiless civil war in which each party committed abuses. There are numerous examples both with the Chetniks but with the Croatian Ustashas and with the Communist Party, but it is true that there was particular violence on the part of the soldiers of the Ravna Gora Movement, so much so that Dragisa Vasic, who was one of the idealogues of the movement, he was the number two between '41 and '43, and he complained to Mr. Mihajlovic about it. There was some behaviour that would shock even the leaders of the movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you have just addressed the issue of what happened during World War II. Through your report but also through witnesses we have heard already on several occasions the issue of the Serb victims during World War II has been addressed. Based on your study, could you tell us how many Serbs were killed during World War II?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's not total agreement as to the number of victims during World War II. We had official figures provided by the Communist regime, that of 1.700.000 victims, but some researchers later on doubted those figures, and based on pre-war demographic figures and statistics, taking into account a potential demographic developments between the '30s and post-war period they came to other figures. For instance, Bogoljub Kocevic, he's a Serb and he provided a higher -- a figure of above 1 million victims, and Mr. Zeljevic, a Croat, carried out a similar study and came to the same conclusion. One assumes that the Communist regime wanted to inflate the number of victims in order to obtain as much reparation, compensation from the Germans after the war, and there was no census or no counting of the victims after the war. It only happened in the '60s. Only then did the authorities look into the matter. That is 20 years after the war, or they came to a figure of 600.000. So it was not completed work. If I take Bogoljub Kocevic's figures one thing is certain, the Serbs were the main victims in Bosnia-Herzegovina because they represent more than half of the victims in Bosnia and Herzegovina which was part of the Independent State of Croatia then. Equally in Croatia, a good part of the victims were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which is the sort of the lower and the higher figure. What kind of bracket could you give us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the Serb victims -- you mean for the whole territory? So if you take as a point -- starting point of 1 million -- I can't remember the figure exactly. Close to half. I have to check in Bogoljub Kocevic's book. I can't right now remember this figure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on what you say, there was 1.700.000 and then other studies speak of 1 million victims. So the lower figure would be more or less 1 million and the higher figure would be 1.700.000.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For all victims, all nationalities included.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what was the overall population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About 14 million inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was it only for all of Serbia or was it for the entire Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For all of Yugoslavia, all nationalities included.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we could assume 1 million out of 14 million inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Roughly so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, among the victims do we know how many civilians there were compared to the number of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's difficult to assess because the Kingdom of Yugoslavia was totally disbanded, broke down into several states. Sometimes you have regular armies, or sometimes you have armies of partisans of resistance. Not all the combatants were registered be that the Yugoslav army in the homeland, the Ravno Gora. It was difficult to count the number of fighters, and it's difficult to give an exact figure because of the situation of a civil war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when you have such figures or this ratio of 1 in 14 inhabitants who was killed, did you try to compare this ratio with other tragedies that occurred in other countries or is Yugoslavia something quite remarkable, as it were, in this ratio of killed to inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is certain that Yugoslavia was one of the countries that was hardest hit by World War II. It has -- it is one of the countries with the highest number of victims together with Poland.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And through all the books that you were able to read by Serb or Croatian authors, or other origins, did this event create a profound trauma within the population, and is it so that everybody would still speak about it years later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is certain that these events traumatised all the populations that were hit by the conflict. Indeed, there were victims on all sides. Of course more so among certain nationalities, but it is true that the Second World War put an end to a certain lifestyle. Until then there was some tolerance among the groups, and this conflict did create a rift between the various populations, Serb, Croat, and Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This may help us see it more clearly. Please continue, Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: In your research regarding the wartime activities of Commander Djujic, did you determine the number of deaths in the Second World War that he was considered responsible for?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commission entrusted with studying the war crimes committed during the war in Yugoslavia established the figures, and he was accused of the deaths -- of being responsible for the death of 1.800.000 people. I'm sorry, that's a mistake. In relation to the total number of victims, 1.800 victims, and his unit intervened in specific areas of the country. 1.800, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter apologises.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Now, did Commander Djujic make a pronouncement regarding the unification of Serb lands in 1989?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1989 he declared that the Serb lands should be retaken control of, referring to the western Serb lands that were situated in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Where was he when he was making this pronouncement?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: In what country was he living at the time?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the United States.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Now, where was it that Commander Djujic appointed Dr. Seselj a Vojvoda?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true. In June --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Was his pronouncement in connection -- I'm sorry, I interrupted the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Was that pronouncement regarding the unification of Serb lands made in connection with his proclamation of Dr. Seselj as a Vojvoda?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. It was when Mr. Seselj held several speeches in the United States representing his political programme and in continuity of all those events. This contact was established between Mr. Seselj and the Chetnik Movement in emigration.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: When we began yesterday, I had asked you to look at the document in your binder labelled as 167. Can you turn to that now? For the record it's been marked as P140. In the first paragraph does Dr. Seselj identify whom he considers to be the eminent predecessors of the Serbian Chetnik Movement?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of this proclamation it is stated that the efforts should be continued of our predecessors, and the names are mentioned of General Draza Mihajlovic, Dragisa Vasic, and Dr. Stevan Moljevic. And once again the Chetnik flag should be hoisted on all Serb lands. So three names are mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Draza Mihajlovic, who was the military leader of the Ravna Gora Movement, the Supreme Commander, and the defence minister of the Yugoslav government in exile, and Dragisa Vasic and Stevan Moljevic were the two leading ideologues of the Ravna Gora Movement.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Was General Mihajlovic subjected to a war crimes trial after the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was convicted and executed in 1946.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me take you to the beginning of the creation of the Serbian Chetnik Movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. You said that General Mihajlovic was sentenced to death. That is what I heard in French. Here in French it says he was executed. Was he executed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who was he sentenced by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By the new Communist regime who -- which organised a trial which was hardly fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what was he accused of in the indictment, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of having collaborated with the Germans and the Italians and of having fought against the liberation movement led by the Communist Partisans. So he was charged with several crimes at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was not sentenced for war crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in fact for war crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was he alone in this trial or were there others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. There were other leaders and officers in the movement. There were also persons who were sentenced in absence and who were not arrested by the Communists. For example, Slobodan Jovanovic who was prime minister in '42 and '43. He was sentenced to 20 years' imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By the Serb jurisdiction in ex-Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This was a Yugoslav Tribunal, a federal one. I can't give you a precise answer, but the scope of the problem related to the whole of Yugoslavia. So it was the central authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: At the bottom the proclamation can you read the inscription above Dr. Seselj's signature?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The president of the patriotic central administration of the Serb Chetnik Movement, Vojvoda Dr. Vojislav Seselj."

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Does the slogan of the Serbian Chetnik Movement appear above -- in the prior paragraph?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There are a few slogans which are traditional. "Freedom and death. Ravna Gora must win." And then "With faith in God for the King and homeland." "Serbia is eternal for as long as its children are loyal for the resurrection of Serbia, of free Serbia."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When it says "For the King," somebody who does not -- is not familiar with the facts may think that it was a royalist movement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time Yugoslavia was a kingdom, so it was a royal army that was loyal to the King at the time. Therefore, the movement in most of its programmatic declarations referred to the King, the Karadjordjevics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the 18th of February, 1991, the date of the document, was the monarchy still in existence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, why then is there a reference to the King?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a reference to the King because the Ravna Gora Movement was in favour of the monarchy and a parliamentary democracy. So a parliamentary monarchy, because Aleksandar Karadjordjevic was living in exile, and it was not possible to bring him back while Slobodan Milosevic was in power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Aleksandar Karadjordjevic was living where, in the United States?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. He was living in Great Britain.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did Commander Djujic have a view on the restoration of the monarchy?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He remained loyal to the monarchy, and he wished to see the restoration of the monarchy in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did Dr. Seselj have a view on the restoration of the monarchy in 1991?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning Mr. Seselj was favourably inclined towards the restoration of the monarchy. That is in 1991, 1992. One notices that he puts a distance between him and the monarchy, and he mentions the possibility of organising a referendum on the question, that is the return of the monarchy, that this should be put to the citizens. And I think that he was severely critical of the successor to the throne. He didn't think that he would be capable of defending his policies.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did the divergent views between Commander Djujic and Dr. Seselj cause problems between them later on?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The relations became problematic after Vojislav Seselj supported informally the powers that be at the time that was led by the Socialist Party of Serbia to such a point that -- that some called him the Red Vojvoda. And Momcilo Djujic disassociated himself from Vojislav Seselj at that time, and a statement in the Serbian press at the time was issued in which he said that Vojislav Seselj had betrayed the monarchy and was collaborating with the Socialist Party that was in power at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What happened to Dr. Seselj's title as a Vojvoda?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was withdrawn, if I am not mistaken, in 1998. Momcilo Djujic regretted the choice he had made in 1989.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let's turn back to the creation of the Serbian Chetnik Movement. Can you identify how the Serbian Chetnik Movement was formed?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning Mr. Seselj formed a party under the movement of the Free Movement of Serbia, and within this organisation there were other parties and movements of the same orientation, one might say. There was Srpska Narodna Odredna, the Serbian Renewal Party formed also in 1990, and Vuk Draskovic was one of the Serb intellectuals who helped rehabilitate the Ravna Gora ideology. And then there was the SNO, and he will associate himself with the Serbian Liberty Movement to form the Serbian Renewal Movement in March 1990. Then very quickly after that differences appeared between Vuk Draskovic and Vojislav Seselj, and at a meeting of the leadership of the movement, of the Serbian Renewal Movement, Vuk Draskovic was expelled from the party, but he wouldn't agree to that and there was a separation, a split, and Vojislav Seselj, within the Serbian Renewal Movement, will form the Chetnik Movement in June 1990. And from that moment on, there was a certain stability within this movement under his leadership. There was some tension at first, but later on the leadership stabilised the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Briefly can you describe the platform of the Serbian Renewal Movement with respect to territories in the west of Yugoslavia where crimes were committed against Serbs during the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The programme of the Serbian Chetnik Movement envisaged the restoration of Serbia within ethnic borders, and this would include Macedonia, Bosnia, Herzegovina, Dubrovnik, Dalmatia, Lika, Kordun, Banja, Slavonia, the region of Baranja. Therefore, roughly speaking the territories that were affected during the Second World War, that is where the Serbs were victimised in the regions, that is the military borders, the Krajinas, which included Lika, Kordun, Banja.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Would you compare, please, the party programme of the Serbian Chetnik Movement with regard to the creation of Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand. What should I compare?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Would you compare that programme with the antecedent from the Serbian Renewal Movement. Was it the same? Was it more specific? Was it different? How do they compare?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is perhaps more precise regarding the definition of territories, but globally the two movements envisaged the same thing, that is the creation of a Greater Serbia. The Serbian Renewal Movement placed greater emphasis on the Serb victims during the Second World War, which would later on be done also by the Serbian Chetnik Movement.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me ask you to look at what is in your binder as tab 83, and it's been marked previously as P27. This is the political platform of the Serbian Chetnik Movement. Let me ask you to look at paragraph 1 of the first page. Does that paragraph define what would be the borders or the territories of a Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a definition of the territory of so-called Serbian territory that should be part of the Serbian democratic state in the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Is this the same programme statement that you have quoted in your report at page 81?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is in fact the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me ask you to look at paragraph 20 of the programme statement. What does paragraph 20 concern?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has to do with the so-called revolt of the Kosovo Albanians and of the way of putting an end to it, because at the time there was much dissatisfaction amongst Kosovo Albanians because the autonomy they had within Yugoslavia had been reduced. In the spring '89 there was an amended to the constitution of the Republic of Serbia that was introduced.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the Serbian Chetnik Movement suggested a certain number of solutions to put an end to this Albanian rebellion, because in the spring of '89 there were numerous demonstrations by Kosovo Albanians. So the Serbian Chetnik Movement wanted to suppress the autonomy of the province and to expel 360.000 Albanian immigrants from Yugoslavian territory. They had entered Yugoslavia after the 6th of April, '41, 1941.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you read the first step regarding expulsion of Albanians.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Immediate expulsion of the 360.000 Albanian emigrants and their offspring; delivery of all those who arrived in Yugoslavia from Albania after the 6th of April, 1941 to the United Nations High Commission for Refugees, as there are so many infinitely richer, vaster and unpopulated countries than Yugoslavia, so let them receive these emigrants, and let them show the humanity."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, what happened on the 6th of April, 1941?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In fact, that is the date when Germany and its allies attacked Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when Germany attacked Yugoslavia, was there an influx of Albanian emigrants?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was -- the country was broken up and a great part of Kosovo became part of Albania that was under Italy. The number of 360.000 Albanians who apparently -- who settled in Kosovo at the time is fairly extravagant figure because the population of Kosovo itself at the time, according to the '31 census, the population was 550.000. In 1939 there was a census, a purely regional one and there were about 670.000, and in 1948 there were about 720.000 inhabitants. So the figure 360.000 added to the total number of the population in 1939, would result in a figure for the population which is far larger in '48. So they must have taken into consideration Serbs who left Kosovo during the Second World War and of the victims of the war. So the official figures, the Yugoslav official figures from the Federal Ministry of the Interior, from a report that was made public in December '88, mentioned 15.000 citizens of Albanian origin who had settled in Yugoslavia between 1941 and 1948 -- 1988. And for the Second World War period, in Kosovo they said there were 3.000 Albanians who were born in Albania and who had settled in Kosovo, and about 500 Albanians who were born in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia that they left this kingdom before the Second World War and settled in Albania and returned to Kosovo between 1941 and 1945.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Milosevic in his decision to reduce the amount of autonomy granted to Kosovo, was he influenced when doing this by Mr. Seselj's party's programme, at least as far as the Albanian question in Kosovo is concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so. Having said that, the Serbian Chetnik Movement programme is far more radical than the programme followed by the Serbian authorities at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An additional question. As for the Kosovo Albanians, the ones who arrived after the 6th of April, 1941, with the passage of time and after 1945, '46, and up until 1991, did they have papers? Did they have nationality? What was their status exactly? Were they still considered to be there illegally? Was the status legal? Did you look into the legal situation, their legal status?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, after the war they were considered to be refugees, some of them at least. There were several waves of immigration. The first wave took place during the Second World War and then in the 50s there was a second wave of Albanian immigration. The Albanians came from Albania and they were fleeing the Enver Hoxha regime. As far as the Albanians born in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia are concerned, Albanians who had left Yugoslavia after the Second World War, they had lost their Yugoslav nationality. They had been stripped of their Yugoslav nationality when they settled in Kosovo. Kosovo was then part of Albania but Kosovo became part of Yugoslavia again at the end of the Second World War, but they were no longer citizens of Yugoslavia. So their status was regulated after the war and several hundred of them maintained the status of refugees. There are about 700 of them who had the status of refugees in 1988.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I've understood you correctly, some still had the status of refugees, but a certain number had Yugoslav nationality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Their situation had been regularised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So they were Yugoslav citizens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They had become Yugoslav citizens.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Were you able to determine an official figure of the number of persons from Albania living in Yugoslavia from 1941 until 1988?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a list. The federal authorities at the time had a list of a -- of 11.000 names, of about 11.000 names but they thought that an additional 4.000 had settled down in Yugoslavia during the period in question. So that would be a total of about 15.000 individuals. At the time when these figures appeared in the press in December'88, these figures weren't contested in Belgrade in Serbia. And it's difficult to imagine that these -- that this figure has underestimated the number of Albanians from Albania who settled in Yugoslavia since there was a police control in Kosovo after the war. So the Communist authorities were in power in Yugoslavia in the spring of 1945. There was an Albanian rebellion which provoked a Yugoslav army reaction at the time, and when Yugoslavia broke with the Soviet Union, Enver Hoxha's Albanians supported Stalin rather than Tito and the Albanians were perceived as potentially dangerous elements, so the police did control the Albanian population at the time, and one might assume that this sentence is fairly precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will go back to the platform now, the political platform of the Serbian Chetnik Movement. The document we have before us, well, what strikes me is that at the very beginning of the text one refers to the restoration of the liberty, independence, and democracy. The question of "territory" is dealt with later. The entire document or other items in the document concern restoring the market economy, the legal system, the judiciary, and paragraph 20 mentions the Albanian issue. The Prosecution emphasises the issue of territory, and you, as our expert today, what would you say that the main objective of this political platform was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at the time the -- Yugoslavia was breaking up, so the debate was about the future of the country, about how to reorganise the country, and so the Serbian Chetnik Movement situates itself within this context and presents its own vision of the future of Yugoslavia and it's the Serbian national question that dominates all political debates at the time. It's the main issue at the time. The Serbian Chetnik Movement was created in June 1990. The -- Croatia was already experiencing certain tensions between the -- its own political authorities and its local Serb population. And as of June 1990, the -- Slobodan Milosevic and Borisav Jovic, who at the time was the president of the Yugoslav Federation, had the idea of cutting off Croatian territory. So it was a natural question that predominated and if Slovenia and Croatia were to become independent it was thought at that point in time Croatian Serbs should exercise their right to self-determination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see this in the document what you have said? Is there clearly stated in the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm explaining a few things about the context, but as for the political programme, there can be certain basic principles that perhaps are not respected by the parties in question. When you have a political programme certain things are carried out, others are not. So item 1A, under item 1A you can see this intention to create a Greater Serbia which would include territory outside of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I notice that the platform includes the phrase "Restoration of a free, independent, and democratic Serbian state in the Balkans." What is the implication from the use of the word "restoration"?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a restoration implies that this state already existed in -- within certain borders. The state of Serbia, such as it had existed since the beginning of the nineteenth century.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Had there ever been a state of Serbia as described in paragraph 1 in history?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Including all these territories? No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me go back to paragraph 20 and ask you whether the platform includes a declaration of a state of war in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact this is one of the measures envisaged.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: How long did the Chetnik Movement -- yes.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a period of less than ten years.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: For a period of at least ten years, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did the Chetnik Movement take a position with respect to the functioning of civilian authorities in institutions in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a matter of -- of suppressing all the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did the Chetnik Movement take a position with regard to establishing a separation zone or a buffer zone between the Albanian state and Serbia?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The programme mentioned a buffer zone at the border with Albania and would extend for -- to a depth of 20 to 50 kilometres, and given its strategic importance for the defence of the country, it -- there shouldn't be any Albanians in that stretch of territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What would be done with Albanians found in that territory when the zone would be established?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says that they should be moved, so perhaps they were part of the 360.000 Albanians who were supposed to depart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why do you say they should have been moved and also receive financial compensation? Why didn't you say that as it says in the text? You didn't mention the compensation. Because that changes everything. It's not the same thing, moving people and not giving them anything, and moving people and providing them with financial compensation.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did the Chetnik Movement take a position about Albanians with Serbian citizenship residing abroad who are involved in a separatist movement?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they wanted to withdraw their Yugoslav nationality and ban them from returning to Kosovo, to Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did the Chetnik Movement take a position about social welfare benefits for persons in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wanted to suppress all forms of social aid since at the time they believed that there was a "rampant" demography amongst the Albanians. They wanted to put an end to this river of demographic growth.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Are you referring to the assertion that those in Kosovo were enjoying a high birth rate?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a reality. Indeed the birth rate of Kosovo Albanians was the highest in Yugoslavia. There was a growth of the Albanian population that was much higher than that of the local Serbian population.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: In the last paragraph does the Chetnik Movement take a position on whether elections should be held?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The programme indeed states that there can't be any elections to be organised in the territory of Kosovo as long as the ethnic structure of the population is not brought back to the levels of the 6th of April, 1941.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you state whether this aspect of the Chetnik programme continued into the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on when the Serbian Radical Party was founded in February in 1991, all this programme, all the points related to Kosovo was taken up and further developed. In fact, many of the points of the Chetnik -- the Serbian Chetnik Movement programme are to be found in the programme of the Serbian Radical Party in February 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Before we turn to that, was Dr. Seselj able to register the Serbian Chetnik Movement as a lawful political party in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In late July 1990 there was an application for registration that was filed by the leadership of the Serbian Chetnik Serb, but it did not achieve its goal because early in 1990 the authorities said that they would not register this political movement because it was associated with their Chetnik Movement of the Second World War, and the leaders of the Chetnik Movement had been convicted for war crimes by the Yugoslav judiciary in '46. This might have shocked the public opinion, the local public opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me ask you to turn to tab 94 in your binder. That's the 65 ter exhibit number. Can you look at the headline of the reprint and tell me what it is?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "An interview with Vojislav Seselj, a new Chetnik Vojvoda."

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: At the back of the article is there a date indicated and a publication? In the Serbian version it would be on the page 21.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This interview was published in the Slovenian weekly called Mladina on the 8th of August, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And what was Mladina?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mladina is a weekly. It was in fact the organ of the youth organisation in Slovenia. It was very critical especially in the second half of the '80s with the then Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: For the Chamber's and Dr. Seselj's reference, that is reprint I have taken from his book "Politics as a challenge of conscience," published in 1993 in Belgrade, and I'd ask that the document be marked, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be MFI P150.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you read out the first question and answer.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Question: Do you think that your acts are leading to an agreement between the Croats and the Macedonians?"

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Now, before the journalist's question there was a statement regarding activities by Dr. Seselj at a monastery. Can you read that statement, please.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "With Vojvoda Seselj, we met him the last time when he was moving the plaque away in the Macedonian monastery Prohor Pcinjski not far from Bujanovac."

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interpreter had not finished so I didn't hear your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What did Dr. Seselj do at the monastery?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this happened on the 3rd of August, 1990. Vojislav Seselj, together with members of his party - I believe there were over 40 people - they went to this monastery, Prohor Pcinjski, which at the border between the Republic of Serbia and Macedonia. This monastery is known as a place where the Macedonian Communist parties and movement decided to establish the Republic of Macedonia and thereby contributing to the Macedonian nation to be recognised. The Serbian Chetnik Movement thought that it was some kind of desecration to put a commemorative plaque about this event of the Second World War. This plaque was then removed by force by the members of the Serbian Chetnik Movement.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you now repeat the question and answer now that we have the context for the question.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Does it seem to you that through your acts you are paving the road towards agreements with the Croats and the Macedonians?"

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: How did Dr. Seselj answer that question?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I don't know what we should negotiate about with the Slovenians and Macedonians, and especially with the Macedonians who are an invented people. There can be no negotiations with them. Macedonia was part of Serbia even before the creation of Yugoslavia, and it was an internationally recognised country."

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What was the journalist's follow-up question and answer?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "And what if the Macedonians do not accept their country being part of a Greater Serbia?" And the answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Well, let them move out then."

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What was the exchange that followed that answer?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Are you afraid of war?" The answer: "With whom?"

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: When the journalist suggested perhaps "With the Croats, for instance," what did Dr. Seselj say?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "With the Croats? Well, when -- when have they fought? All they can do is talk a lot, raise a lot of dust, make a fuss, and that is all."

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: In this interview did Dr. Seselj articulate the borders of Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He does mention in answering the next question: "The borders of Serbia, Karlobag, Karlovac, the Kupa River, and Virovitica."

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did Dr. Seselj express an opinion on the need for a transitional period and a national army?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's against any transitional period. He is of the view that it has to be created very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did the journalist question Dr. Seselj about the new name of his political party then, the Serbian Chetnik Movement?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What was the question asked?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "You shouldn't think that this hasn't been thought through. Don't you think it's a lack of reflection to call your party the Serbian Chetnik Movement considering the opinion formed with regard to the Chetniks?"

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And what was Dr. Seselj's answer?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I think that such a name evokes only the best associations among the Serbs, because the Chetniks have always been fighters for freedom and for the defence of the homeland."

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What happened when Dr. Seselj was not able to register the Serbian Chetnik Movement as a legal political party?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for this organisation it was difficult to do anything, including to organise public gatherings since the authorities could easily ban such gatherings because this movement had not been legally, officially registered. But this did not prevent the Serbian Chetnik Movement from organising various gatherings in spite of their prohibitions that had been expressed. This movement finds itself in a difficult situation. It is not registered. Therefore, it is difficult for it when the first elections are about to be organised in December 1990 in Serbia. So Mr. Seselj cannot run as a candidate for the Chetnik Movement to the presidential election. He will run as an independent candidate based on a group of citizens, even though indeed all his speeches show that as a candidate he does -- he did represent at the time the Serbian Chetniks. So the way out is to create the Serbian Radical Party in February 1991. Under this name of the Serbian Radical Party, this party will be acknowledged by the authorities in March 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your help, I'd like to find an answer to the following question I have in mind. This is an interview which deals with the end with the independence of Slovenia. At the time were there Serbs in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very few. There were many Serbs who had come to the republic to work, but there's no population --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many in percentage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know exactly but very few. Some thousands. But Slovenia was the most homogeneous republic, nationally speaking, so it basically had no problem with national minorities both for the powers that be in Belgrade but also for the nationalists in Slovenia was no problem. And Milosevic thought that he could let go of Slovenia as quickly as he could in that way because there was no territorial claims between Serbia and Slovenia. In this way, Serbia could then resolve the territorial issues with the other republics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the fact that Slovenia would become independent, would be let go, was that not opening Pandora's box in which other countries like Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina would sort of rush into?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If you let go of one country, that opens the way, the door for other proclamations of independence. Indeed it did favour other republics to leave Yugoslavia since one republic had been let go. But Milosevic's will was in fact to have Yugoslavia comprising all the other republics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This journalist who hears this answer about the independence of Slovenia finished the interview with the following question: He asked him what he thought of the idea of a confederation. What do you think of this question as it was put? Was the journalist not surprised by the fact that this independence would cause no problem, because he asked whether there could not be a confederation, like Slovenia plus Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time when there is a mention made of confederation, it would include the six republics of the Yugoslav Federation, but the free elections had already taken place in April 1990 in Slovenia. This is now in August following the elections, and there are powers in place that are more in favour of a Yugoslav confederation. But in fact Yugoslavia was already a sort of confederation. Formally it was a federation, but the powers of the republics were already quite important with important prerogatives, and there was a rather weakened central federal power which brought certain international organisations like the International Monetary Fund to sort of try and organise a federation to try and repay the debt. So already we were in a confederal context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have just said something that may not be relevant but in my view could have some impact on the future. You said that the federal power was weak. Could you be more specific about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As of the end of the '60s and in the early '70s, the Yugoslav Federation was reformed. It gave a great deal of autonomy to the republics. This reform of the federation went hand-in-hand with the reform of the league of the Communists in Yugoslavia, and eventually each of the leagues in each of the republics became more or less autonomous. In other words, the Congress of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia had to take into account the decisions made by each of the Congresses of the republican league. So you had federation or a confederalisation at the level of the state but also at the level of the party. Each of the republics had their own economic policies. They could make debts with foreign banks. Each republic had its own system of Territorial Defence. So at the federal level you mainly at the central level you had the Yugoslav Army that had remained a federal army, but when it came to external relations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether you have knowledge about economic matters, but now you tackle the issue of debts for each of the republics, but wasn't it Belgrade central bank that would make sure that the monetary system could continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was the central bank. But after that at political level many decisions were made at the level of the republics without there being any real sort of cohesion with the central powers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to have to have a break. It's 10.00. We shall reconvene in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing's resumed. Ms. Dahl, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I ask something of the witness? Sorry, Ms. Dahl. What was the reason for maintaining the structure of the Yugoslav confederation when all the republics wanted to become independent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I pointed out earlier on, I said that there was a trend towards confederalisation of Yugoslavia since the late 1960s, a series of reforms materialised in the change of the constitution in 1974. In 1990, 1991, Croatia and Slovenia are the two republics to advocate this concept of confederalisation of Yugoslavia while Serbia at the time was against this process and wanted, rather, that the central power be strengthened. So we have basically two main options that oppose each other. There is this project of advanced confederalisation advocated by Slovenia and Croatia and on the other hand, a process of re-centralisation advocated by Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Another question regarding the Chetnik Movement: What was the reason why the movement was not officially recognised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The very name of the movement had the word "Chetnik" in it which meant that there was a connection with the Chetnik Movement of the Second World War, and it was deemed that this could be shocking for those who had participated in the national liberation war on the side of the Communist partisans who took power in 1945.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, basically, it was for ideological reasons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was held -- you have this decision that says the Second World War Chetnik Movement has been disbanded, that its members -- its leaders had been convicted and that therefore the new Chetnik Movement could not be recognised; so basically for ideological reasons, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Before the break we were discussing the failure of the Chetnik Movement to get itself registered. Did that preclude Dr. Seselj from participating himself in the elections in December 1990?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I said earlier on, he ran as a candidate proposed by a group of citizens. The problem was that he was convicted in October to a sentence -- a prison sentence of some 15 days, if I'm not mistaken. So he didn't have that much time to prepare for the election campaign.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What position did Dr. Seselj take in the election campaign regarding Croatia seceding from the republic?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the time he presented the main ideas of the Serbian Chetnik Movement. This idea was that in the event of the independence of Croatia, the territories populated by Serbs must be removed from that republic, detached from it with the idea of establishing the western border of Serbia on the line Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Have you quoted Dr. Seselj's campaign positions in your report?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me ask you to turn to page 83.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is a quotation dating back to the time of the election campaign which tallies with what I've just said. It is a warning to the Croats and more specifically to the political chief of the time in Croatia, Franjo Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And what did Dr. Seselj say?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a nutshell, he says that the Croats can separate themselves from Yugoslavia. They can create an independent state, associate themselves with another state, but they must know that at no cost or unless there are -- there's new blood or further rivers of blood, they can take away from us any part of the territory that contains Serbian villages, Serbian mass graves, sites where Serbs were massacred, pits that were -- Serbs were thrown in. They will never allow camps where Serbs were imprisoned such as Jasenovac or Serbian churches that were destroyed. We will never allow this, he said. So that's this idea that if Croatia became independent the Serbs could exercise their right to self-determination, the Serbs living in the territory of Croatia, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Does Dr. Seselj consider that Croatia has a basis for becoming an independent state?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In most of his statements Mr. Seselj expresses a will to present the Croats as being weak, being cowards, basically as not having a very strong statehood tradition.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm looking at page 84. Have you quoted a particular description that Dr. Seselj used in this campaign?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you read that out at the bottom of the page, beginning "The Croats are not a historical nation."

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I see. "The Croats are not a historical nation. Consider the Czechs and the Germans, for instance, Czech is synonymous with coward, while the Germans are a warrior nation. The same goes for the Serbs and the Croats. The Croats are a depraved nation. I have yet to meet a decent Croat." This is an interview that was given to Tanjug, the main Yugoslav press agency at the time, and this interview was later published in the Red Tyrant from Dedinje, a book that was published.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Who is the publisher of that book?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is ABC Glas, it's a publishing house that published all the works by Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: In Dr. Seselj's campaign for the 1990 election, did he use his view of the negotiations for the Treaty of London to justify his territorial positions?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. I noted that there's -- he keeps having this reference to the Treaty of London of 1915 since 1989 which is supposed to trace the western borders along the Karlobag-Virovitica line and this assertion was repeated on several occasions. This western border is part of Vojislav Seselj's discourse, and it's an important one at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me ask you to look at your map number 10 which we've marked as P148.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please, before we look at map number 10. We were at page 84 in your report and you thought it useful to indicate in your report -- to mention this interview with Radio Kakaj [phoen] in 1991. This was published in a book he wrote with the title "Brankovic came out of his grave," published in 1994. This is a rather lengthy text written by Mr. Seselj himself, and it seems to say the following -- with your help, I would like to understand what he meant to say. His premise was that Yugoslavia had stopped existing and ceased to exist, and he added "Only Serbia will remain." So this sentence conveys the impression that the Yugoslav state, as it existed at -- ceased to exist since Slovenia had become independent and Croatia was on the horizon, and he added this: "Serbia will remain. The Kingdom of Yugoslavia is the legal successor," he said, "of the Kingdom of Serbia." And he proceeds in his legal demonstration saying this: "Only Serbia as a state can be the legal successor of Yugoslavia." And of course this is his Yugoslavia, he says: "There is no Yugoslavia any longer since Yugoslavia no longer existed as it became Yugoslavia in 1945. Now we have the Kingdom of Serbia," he said. And he proceeded with this analysis by saying this: "In accordance with the provisions of the Treaty of London --" this is just a hypothesis he put forward, he said, it was possible to have a western border for Serbia. And I think every word counts here. He says this: "It can, and when you say it can, it's just a hypothesis. It's not something that you impose." And he says: "It can follow the Karlobag line if we want it to be a historical and strategic border." I think this sentence says it all. In his view he observes that there is no Yugoslavia any longer, then that the Kingdom of Serbia or Serbia must be the successor unless, of course, there was a new King, but then the legal basis, in his view, would be this famous Treaty of London of 1915. And in a second stage he expresses the idea of this border Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica. So I see that as a hypothesis in his view. And he added this, he said: "If we want it to be an ethnic, historical and strategic border." So this is my reading of it. In your view, what did he mean in saying so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time this was an interview given in September 1991. Yugoslavia was then not totally disbanded or dismantled, even though Croatia and Slovenia had proclaimed their independence, but this is an ongoing process controlled by the European Community of the time, and the independence will only be acknowledged in early 1992, at least for Croatia. I think it's January 1992 when Germany, among other countries, decided to recognise the independence of Croatia. Therefore, Yugoslavia has not totally disappeared at the time, and it is said here that this western border can be -- it's one of many quotations in which things are less presented as hypothesis than in other texts you can read that the western border must be that. So this is one in scores of quotations you could find in all the interviews Seselj gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you say that there are quotations that are much more affirmative.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whilst acknowledges -- one acknowledging that here it is presented in the form of a hypothesis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But you said this interview was given in September 1991, and in his statement he says the moment Yugoslavia ceases to exist because there's an ongoing process. That is what he says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right, when Yugoslavia ceases to exist. And obviously we are approaching the end of Yugoslavia. But before Yugoslavia was formed, there were two independent states only. That is Serbia and Montenegro that were recognised by the Congress of Berlin in 1878.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I come back to Croatia very quickly. This thesis that it is not a nation, that it is not a state, he raises the issue by saying we will see -- we see the concern of the international community to regulate Croatia. He envisages several hypotheses. He says that perhaps the Italians, maybe the Austrians, maybe the Hungarians. He envisages various things, but he is not determined regarding the existence of this Croatian state.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But Croatia should be formed outside this western frontier line, Karlovac-Ogulin-Karlobag-Virovitica. It doesn't -- he doesn't concern himself with what will happen behind that line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But to the extent that he says that this line which is of concern to Croatia, of course, but he says in his speech that there is no Croatian state and if there is no Croatian state then one can wonder what he actually meant. What do you think about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Republic of Croatia was a component of the federal state, but he is contesting that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Republic of Croatia at the time was one of the republics of the federation. It is an administrative entity in a sense from the international standpoint. The Republic of Croatia at the time was not internationally recognised. It was ex-Yugoslavia that was internationally recognised.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but this process that is ongoing is going to define the rules for the recognition of the components of Yugoslavia. The Badinter Commission is establishing criteria for recognition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but at the moment he's speaking the Republic of Croatia was still not recognised; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was one of the republics of ex-Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We are in agreement, yes. But judging by what he says, though it was one of the republics of ex-Yugoslavia from the point of view of a state he's contesting the notion of state and even of a nation. He says the Croats are not an historic nation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In many of his writings and his statements he ignores the fact that the Croats had a state in the Middle Ages. They were part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, yes, and the Croatian state of the time was integrated with Hungary and that was the case until the First World War.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But he says that in 1102 it was a state, he said that. He says since 1102, the Croats never had a state, which means that before that they did have one. And in his view between 1102 and 1991, there was no state in the sense of an internationally recognised state.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Kingdom of Croatia was at the time a component of the Kingdom of Hungary, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I am asking you these questions because you are the expert and not me, and I am trying to understand the meaning of what he wrote in order to integrate all this into a much broader scope, and that is the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let us go to your map number 10, which has been previously marked as P148. Looking at the western borders in the political context in which this map was published in August 1990, can you draw a conclusion whether or not those borders could be achieved peacefully?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With difficulty, in view of the fact it is including territory with non-Serb populations which enter in the concept of a Greater Serbia. Bosnia-Herzegovina is populated by Bosniaks, Muslims and Croats. In Macedonia there is the Macedonian nation. In any event, people who defined themselves as being Macedonian and which would not fit into the -- which would not accept the ideology of Greater Serbia, the more so in view of the memories from the Second World War this concept had meaning for -- certain meaning for some people evoking conflicts. It is not a project that non-Serb populations could adhere to of these regions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but from his standpoint he is saying that there is no national consciousness on the part of the Croats. He's denying the nationhood of the Macedonians. In his point of view, these people, in particular the Croats, are not going to fight because they're not warriors, they are Croats. Therefore, in the light of these -- this discourse, I still cannot see that the means of getting hold of this territory would be military means. Could you elaborate on this particular point and provide some clarification, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we take the example of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in Bosnia and Herzegovina there are three ethnic communities, the Bosniaks, the Muslims, the Serbs, and the Croats. The Serbs who until after the Second World War were -- had a relative majority moved from the first place to the second place, the Muslim group becoming the predominant, the largest ethnic community. So we have a territory with mixed -- with a mixed population, and their views of the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina are not identical, and the Croats of Bosnia and the Bosniaks of Bosnia do not accept the idea of Bosnia-Herzegovina being included in a Greater Serbia. So I don't see how this objective could be achieved, because each national community had its own national project, and these were competing projects frequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is your opinion, but from his point of view I would like to know what the means are. Did he envisage military means or proceeding from his viewpoint, which may be erroneous but that was his point of view, could he have envisaged a path that would be a non-military path?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1990 we can see that Serb volunteers are beginning to be organised and sent to Croatia. So the Chetnik Movement itself has a military dimension to it in the sense that creating a party called a Chetnik Party, this very word meant a military activity, and to resolve this question when the Chetnik Movement became a component part of the Radical Party, so it was no longer a purely political party. In spring 1991, we see volunteers being sent by the Serbian Radical Party. So there were military activities undertaken within the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another problem at this stage.
