I would like to ask you whether the Chetnik Movement had this military dimension and these war-like intentions only when there was already a war-like situation as there was during the Second World War, and this entailed their active participation in the war, or in the spring of 1991, yes, there already was a conflict in ex-Yugoslavia, and therefore whether outside a conflict that had already started he may have nonetheless envisaged other means, other methods of -- of gaining control of these territories. That is just what I wanted to clear up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I follow up to this question, which is a fundamental one and a very important one, and I thank the Judge for putting it. In the position of Mr. Seselj and his political party, was the objective sought or could the objective sought have been achieved by political means or, in your own view, this could only be achieved by military means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On several occasions he says that there can be no negotiations with the Macedonians or the Croats, which limits the possibility of negotiation. From the moment one wishes to include in Greater Serbia territories which are populated by minority Serbs in Western Slavonia, the Serbs only represented about 25 per cent of the population. Clearly there cannot be adhesion of the non-Serb population there to this project of a Greater Serbia. You cannot achieve such a project which is being addressed mainly to the Serbs without involving the adhesion of non-Serb populations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand what you're trying to tell us, but we are faced with the following problem: Before the years when the conflicts broke out in this region there was ex-Yugoslavia which functioned under a Communist regime where Serbs, Croats, Muslims lived apparently on good terms. Then comes the "dismantling" of ex-Yugoslavia. Some people like him and others are going to raise the national issue, and this national issue can have political solutions or military solutions, and our concern is to find out whether when -- when he made this map, when he held these speeches and when he formed the Serbian Radical Party, was the military option the only option, or perhaps there may have been other options and specifically the Badinter Commission option which we'll have this issue of a referendum in Bosnia and Herzegovina and to see what they wanted or not. The question is whether a democratic means could have been the follow-up to this political programme. The Chetnik Movement did have a military connotation at the beginning, but as my colleague said so well this was the case during the Second World War but in 1990, 1991, and 1992, there's no worldwide conflict ongoing, and therefore are you almost certain that this could only be resolved by military means and that political means, the method of self-determination, referendum, elections, could not have perhaps allowed the implementation or realisation of a Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I know myself is that as of 1989 when Mr. Seselj was in the United States, he mentions the idea of the amputation of a part of Croatia and punishing the Croats for the crimes they committed during the Second World War. Therefore, this idea of amputation of Croat territory existed already then. Then there are several processes that are ongoing in Croatia. There is a Serb population that started to mobilise itself already in 1989 in the context of the celebration of the 600th anniversary of the Kosovo battle. Then there were the parliamentary elections of April 1990, which brought to power the Croatian Democratic Community, which is a nationalist party, which is going to call in question the position of the Serbs within Croatia to the extent that the Serbs who were considered a constituent nation of the Republic of Croatia are going to lose that status and become a simple national minority. And therefore, from that moment on there is a -- a will on the part of the Serbs in Croatia to detach themselves from Croatia and to detach a part of the territory in which they are more or less the majority. The Republic of Croatia and their authorities react and hence all the incidents around the police stations, which both parties wish to take control of. And in the spring of 1991, there's a deterioration of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this deterioration of the situation that you have just referred to, we can understand it from the standpoint of the Serbs of Croatia who are seeing what is happening, but how does this directly affect Dr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the moment there is tension, he sends volunteers or units of volunteers belonging to the Serbian Radical Party to Croatia, to Slavonia, and there are the first conflicts in the beginning of May 1991 in the small location called Borovo Selo, and it is in this context that his volunteer units intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he sends them either as defenders or in an offensive sense? In a defensive or offensive sense?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my view there are both aspects. In his speeches he speaks of defending the Serbs from the new Croatian authorities, but behind that there is a political will to redefine the frontiers of this region, and therefore to make efforts to achieve or to approach the line defined by his programme and that is Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica. But this policy, this objective is also shared the League of Communists of Serbia which in July of 1999 became the Socialist Party of Serbia, and there are many actors at various levels in the party to have control over the security services, the police and the army, and others like the Radical Party who are sending units of volunteers to Croatia. There is a kind of convergence from the moment that Croatia declares its independence. There is a will to detach a part of the territory of Croatia that is inhabited by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Listening to you about the amputation of part of Croatia, it is apparently the Croats who began. It is not the Serbs and Croats who generated the incidents first. Will you please explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The tensions started in '89 when they're celebrating the 600th anniversary of the Kosovo battle. In Kosovo itself there was large gathering. Slobodan Milosevic held a speech that has become famous. But in July '89 there was a large gathering of Serbs in the Krajina region. Many Serbs from other republics, from Bosnia, Serbia arrived. They came there. They were there were about 60.000 persons who gathered there, and this gathering, the idea of a Greater Serbia within -- of a Serbian entity within Croatia was mentioned. In the Chetnik immigration press, reference was made to a Serbian entity within Croatia, to the creation of such an entity, and as of that point in time tension developed between the powers or authorities in Croatia and part of the Serbian population in Croatia. In '89 elections hadn't been held yet and Tudjman wasn't yet in power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my last question before I give the floor back to Ms. Dahl. If the former Yugoslavia had simply been replaced by a Greater Serbia, well, was this something that could have been carried out or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, one should bear in mind something very important. Serbia is one of the most heterogeneous republics in the former Yugoslavia. According to the figures, in 1991 there's about 60 per cent of Serbs in Serbia. It's a small percentage in comparison to Slovenia, for example. So if you create a Greater Serbia, the proportion of Serbs will diminish significantly. If you take these borders here, you can't be sure that the Serbs would be in the majority in such a state. So if one wants to create a Greater Serbia, it's not to have the Serbs as a minority in such a Serbia. There were 66 per cent of Serbs in Serbia at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understand things correctly, this Greater Serbia could never have been within the borders of the former Yugoslavia. It would have had to be a state the size of which was much smaller.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Greater Serbia excludes Slovenia, and it only has in mind a smaller Croatia. But if you have a look at the map, it's the -- represents all of Yugoslavia without Slovenia and part of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Judge Antonetti, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me bring up a map that illustrates the KOKV line. It's map number 5 in our map book with the ERN number 06046937. I'll give you the 65 ter number in just a moment. It's at 7006. Mr. Tomic, can you identify the red border that surrounds the republics on this map?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This map is more precise. It shows Greater Serbia in greater precision than was the case in the journal of the Serbian Chetnik Movement.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can we have the map given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number P151.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: So to --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection, Your Honours. This is a case of evident falsification, this map of Greater Serbia comes from the London Times. It's not from the journal Velika Srbija, the Greater Serbia. The Karlovac-Virovitica-Karlobag line is depicted differently in Velika Srbija. I don't mean the other map because that was a clumsily drawn map for the title page of the second issue of Velika Srbija but the Prosecution does have an original map of Velika Srbija, Greater Serbia, from the journal Velika Srbija or rather, Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let's look at map number 6 then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Witness, this map is from The Times. It has been contested. Its lines -- the lines drawn have been contested. What would you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This map appeared in -- the map in Velika Srbija is more of a drawing. It's not a very precise map if you compare it with a geographic map compiled in accordance with the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the map we have in front of us, the map that is being contested, this map which is also called a map of Greater Serbia, does this map correspond to the map that was published in the Radical Party's publication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if Karlobag is the point of departure and if we pass through Ogulin and Karlovac and then Virovitica, then the problem is -- although I had can't see everything very clearly on the screen, I can't see the names of the locations, but if that is the route that the line follows, the line at the west that the Chetnik Movement designs, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, please instruct the Prosecution to show you the original map of Greater Serbia from our journal. Sisak is included in Greater Serbia in here, and that's not the case in that -- in the other map. And many other places. This is an inauthentic map. The Prosecution has the original map from our journal. They have the original map but not the drawing that resembles a caricature that they were using a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl, apparently the Prosecution has the original map in its possession.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me ask the registrar to bring up the Exhibit 2 -- 7007. I'm sorry. It's map number 6 in the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which is the original map, because Mr. Seselj is asking us to show the original map that appeared in the publication. Is this the map in question?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me ask Mr. Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you identify this map?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This looks like the map that appeared in Velika Srbija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I'll put the question to Mr. Seselj. Is this the map that appeared in the publication, the map that we can see on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is the original map, although it seems a bit stretched here. It must be something that's been done deliberately, but the projection -- in terms of its projection it seems a bit stretched, but it is the original map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So this is the original. Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: So to return to the questions that the Bench was asking you, if the borders of Serbia were expanded along the line indicated in this map of Serbia, what would happen to the proportion of the population that is Serb if the inhabitants all stayed in their -- their places of residence? That is to say, if there were no population expulsions or exchanges upon the redrawing of the borders to correspond with what Dr. Seselj advocated.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think one should have all the right statistics, carry out a detailed examination, take into consideration the census of 1991 or even better the census of 1981, but I believe that the Serbs in this Greater Serbia wouldn't have been in the majority, or they would have barely been in the majority. They would have had about -- they were the -- represent about 50 per cent of the population, because in Bosnia-Herzegovina the Serbs represented about 33 per cent of the population. The Muslim Bosnians and the Croats were in the majority. And in addition --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting you, but you're saying something that is quite important here that shouldn't escape anyone's attention. You have just said, if I have understood you correctly, when looking at the map we have before us, the so-called map of Greater Serbia as seen by the Radical Party, well, you have said, if we have a look at the demographic composition of the inhabitants inhabiting the territory of this map, well, in your opinion you would say that the Serbs wouldn't be in the majority.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be about 50 per cent. So they would barely be in the majority. I can't give you a precise answer. You should take into consideration censuses of each and every municipality. But the Serbs weren't in the majority in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and they weren't in the majority in Macedonia, because the Macedonians, the Slavs in Macedonia say they're Macedonians. There are several thousand Serbs in Macedonia. In this state, well, within the borders you also have Croats in Slavonia and in Krajina. So in fact on the basis of the figures that appeared in certain studies, I can't give you precise references, but on the basis of these studies I think it's quite clear that the Serbian population would represent about 50 per cent of the total and that would pose a problem in Greater Serbia because could the Serbian nation find itself in such a weak position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This notion of a Greater Serbia if you have a look at the territorial aspect of this notion without thinking about ethnic groups, well, in that case could there be a Greater Serbia, although in purely territorial nature. The ethnic composition would be such as it was. You would have 50 per cent of Serbs and 50 per cent of non-Serbs. Or, and this is the Prosecution's case, the Greater Serbia such as it is represented in the map, would this Greater Serbia only be feasible if there were population movements, if the population was moved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Movements in 1991, for example, there were population movements that were envisaged. In numerous interviews given to the press, Mr. Seselj mentioned the idea of moving. The Serbs would be behind the Karlobag-Ogulin-Virovitica line, so that concerns Serbs living in the Zagreb and Rijeka region. In his opinion they couldn't continue to live in an independent Croatian state. As a result they would have to be moved to the interior of Serbia and there should be an exchange of population with the Croats from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you have just said is very important. What he said is that on the basis of the Serbian situation in Croatia, these Serbs in Croatia should go to the Greater Serbia and this would be done by organising an exchange. Croats from the Greater Serbia would leave. They'd be forced to do so or would they do so voluntarily or they wouldn't leave? What would be the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, when you live in a certain place and if you're quite well there, you don't want to leave the place. You have your personal and professional life there, your family life there so this process can hardly be a process that most people would accept, this process of having a population exchange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's your conclusion then. Such a transfer, such an exchange would only be problematic, because force would have to be used to move the population.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A population exchange, well, if it's defined -- who defines it? Is it an agreement between states? Is it the politics of fait accompli? In 1991 in an interview this idea was mentioned, this idea of a population exchange. Seselj mentioned 200.000 Serbs in Zagreb and 30.000 in Rijeka, they could no longer live in a Croatian state. They would have to be moved to Serbia and then you would have to organise an exchange of population, send Serbs to the Greater Serbia and the Croats to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a problem with regards to your observation on the Greater Serbia as devised by Mr. Seselj and also about the ratio of Serbs that apparently would have made up this Greater Serbia, some 50 per cent. When you mentioned this percentage, do you have in mind the Orthodox Serbs or do you also have other Serbs in mind of other faith?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have in mind the people who identified themselves as Serbs during the census, because the people were asked for their nationalities. So one should not define for them what nationality they are. They self-identified. They self-defined their nationality. So I take account of the census carried out by the state authorities in which people clearly identified their national belonging.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I have a question regarding Bosnia and Herzegovina. Were there Serbs who identified themselves as being of Serb nationality, or did they identify themselves as Bosnians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Bosnia the three nations, the Serb, Croat, and Muslim, were regarded as the constituent peoples of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So they identified themselves as being Muslim, then Muslim nation was the official name. So they were either that or Croat or Serb, but other could also say they were Yugoslavs, and there were other smaller national groups within Bosnia and Herzegovina. So at the time there is no super national Bosnian identity as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in your calculation to arrive at 50 per cent of the Greater Serbia, you also include the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who had chosen to identify themselves as such?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because I take into account the people who declared they were Serbs in -- during the census in all these territories mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apparently there are two census, one in 1981, another one in 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Yugoslavia every ten years, in the first year of each ten years. So you had '61, '71, '81, and '91.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In 1981 when there was a census in the former Yugoslavia, was there also a Yugoslav category?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you roughly, as far as you remember, remember the ratios?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were not so many Yugoslavs. Those who declared they were Yugoslavs came from mixed families, mixed couples. So they were more numerous in some areas where you had mixed population as was the case in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but that has to be checked. I can't remember all the figures, all the -- all the population ratios. It was some 5 to 8 per cent depending on the area. But the Yugoslav national identity was never supported by the communist powers. It was about identifying national identities, Slovenian, Muslim, Croat, Macedonian, Montenegrin, but they didn't want to create a Yugoslav nation as was the case in the first Yugoslavia because they thought that this idea -- that was the point of view of the Communist rulers at the time. They thought that that would go more towards the interest of the Serbs who were more numerous within in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This 1981 or 1991 census within Yugoslavia, what was -- what were the percentages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Yugoslavs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some slightly over 30 per cent, 36 per cent, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thirty-six per cent. As to the remainder, how many Croats, for instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that in the first Yugoslavia they amounted to some 22 per cent so it could be 18 to 20 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't give you any precise figure. I think there was 44 per cent in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. There are also Muslim Slavs in the Republic of Serbia, in the Sandzak area, for instance, in particular. Some 2 million inhabitants in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So 1.8, 1.9, but, you know, I can't remember all the figures because we covered a very long period and you'd need to have statistical charts to be really -- to work properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you feel, Mr. President, that my objection is inappropriate, I will withdraw it immediately, but I must draw your attention that the Prosecutor, with the help of the witness, is confusing you. This is the ideal projection of Greater Serbia. These are territories where stokavian is being spoken excluding the Albanians and the Hungarians. When I advocated exchanges of population, this related to the existing Serbia and the existing Croatia. They are confusing you and I think they're doing so on purpose. This is the ideal projection, much larger than Republika Srpska and the Serb Krajina. There would be more than 2 million who declared themselves as Muslims and more than 2 million who consider themselves Croats and I consider them to be Serbs of Catholic faith. This is just the ideal projection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The accused Mr. Seselj has just expressed his point of view regarding the population issue. What do you have to say to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this is supposed to be the place where stokavian is spoken, I think cakavian is spoken in Dalmatia, in Split and above. I think I heard cakavian being spoken below the Karlobag line and the Dalmatian coast. So it's not just the stokavian area that is shown here or where stokavian is spoken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will have an opportunity to go back to this later on. Please proceed, Ms. Dahl. Yes. We'll have an opportunity. You can proceed Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Let's have a P number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Witness, I have a question because you understand that we did take up a lot of time, but it was necessary to do so. Obviously we're not going to finish your testimony this week. Can you come back on Monday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Oh, sorry, sorry. I said Monday. I should have said Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: May I please have a P number for the map which is map 6, 65 ter Exhibit 7007.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number P152.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Very briefly let's look at P26, which shows the Greater Serbia border imposed on the ex-Yugoslavia republics. Let me ask Mr. Tomic if he can confirm the outlines on this map. Mr. Tomic, looking at this map can you confirm whether the borders illustrated here in the red shading conform to the map of Greater Serbia published by the Serbian Chetnik Movement?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They appear to be very similar.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: To avoid any doubt, has there ever been a western border historically through Karlobag, Ogulin, Karlovac, and Virovitica?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of this boundary was in -- a boundary in the 16th and 17th centuries between the Austrian Empire and the Ottoman Empire. Karlobag as is indicated by the name Karl comes from Charles of Habsburg and Karlovac is also a fortified town created in the 16th century, so that's the same root, you have Karl as in Charles, but we are in the area of the military boundaries. But at the time the line was not totally identical, at least up to Karlovac. Then I can't guarantee that it was exactly the same further north.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Now, in the period of time between 1990 and 1993 when Dr. Seselj was advocating this configuration of a Greater Serbia, did that concept enjoy popular support by persons who did not identify themselves as Serbs?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that members of national minorities of other non-Serb communities would have supported such a policy. Of course there may be cases, isolated cases of individuals who may be from a minority group or support this policy, but often they're very connected to Serbs. They live in symbiosis with the local Serbian population so they're very close to Serbs. But this policy can only be supported by Serbs. I can't see any other popular support for it coming from non-Serb populations in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Would you say the Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina welcomed the idea of a homogenous Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we talking about 1990, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yes, that period of time.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be that some Muslims may have expressed themselves in favour of the project, but there wouldn't be many of them. It would remain very much a marginal phenomenon.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let us turn --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this respect when Mr. Seselj testified in the Milosevic trial and this testimony has been admitted to our case file because it was so decided by the Trial Chamber, Mr. Seselj quoted many Muslims who actually identified themselves as Serbs. Are you aware of very well-known individuals of Muslim intellectuals who before regarding themselves as Muslim would say they were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was roughly the case until after the Second World War when the Muslim nation was not recognised. So the Muslim Slavs would identify themselves as not being determined or some would indeed say of themselves that they were Croats or Serbs of Muslim faith. But the bulk, the majority of Muslim in Bosnia-Herzegovina said that they were not determined or undecided. There may be a minute portion of them who would have identified as Serbs or Croats depending on the local position, the local history, or the family history. Most intellectuals of repute, Bosnian Muslims of the time, would support the SDA, Alija Izetbegovic's party, or possibly other parties, the one that is later to become the social -- the democrat -- the social democratic party coming from the League of Communists in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let us return to the creation of the Serbian Radical Party in 1991. Let me ask you to turn to tab 144 in your notebook. To summarise briefly for the Chamber, this is a compilation of materials reprinted in one of Dr. Seselj's books, and I would like to draw your attention to the founding Assembly speech, the manifesto, and the basic programme as well as the statute. Can you briefly describe what led to the decision by Dr. Seselj to form the Serbian Radical Party in 1991?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two points need to be made that I mentioned before. There was the Serb Chetnik Movement that was not recognised by the authorities of the country, and this was a problem for the extension and development of the movement, and in addition there was the popular Radical Party which was formed at the time of the introduction of a multi-party system, and it was divided as of 1991 because it was not elected to the Assembly of Serbia. So Vojislav Seselj is going to come to an agreement with one of the leaders of the People's Radical Party, that is Tomislav Nikolic in order to form together -- for them to form together a new political party. At first they were going to keep the name People's Radical Party, but at the founding Congress the party will be named the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have mentioned a name that is quite well known, on line 65. You mentioned the name Tomislav Nikolic. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He originally lived in Kragujevac and at the time he was member of the People's Radical Party and later he was to become one of the main leaders of The Radical Party, and today he is the vice-president of the Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what was his training? Is he a lawyer, a university person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so. He is not a jurist. I have forgotten what his profession is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when this party was formed, was he a strong figure in the party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The People's Radical Party was a well-known party at the time, because it was one of the main parties at the end of the 19th century, and up to the 20s in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia as well. Having said that, it is a party that did not succeed in imposing itself at the first free elections in Serbia in December 1990. I don't know enough regarding the situation within that party, and I think after the elections it split up and formed sections, and a certain section joined with the Serb Chetnik Movement to form the Radical Party. It was a marginal entity because it was not voted into parliament.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Looking at Dr. Seselj's speech at the founding Assembly, can you identify what commitments Dr. Seselj makes clear with regard to the parties' positions?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What page are you referring to, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I took the Serbian text out of my binder. It's at page 6 of the English translation, and it's in all capitals, "What are our commitments." And Dr. Seselj's speech appears under CVII, under the caption "In his second address to delegates and guests Dr. Seselj said ..." If I can get my assistant to help with the Serbian text, I can point you to the precise page. Have you located the passage?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What are the commitments that Dr. Seselj makes as part of the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wishes to continue the activities of the Serbian People's Radical Party formed in 1881 and which was founded by Nikola Pasic and was the leading party at the time. He was one of the main leaders of the government in the Kingdom of Serbia, later the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, and he claims that the programme of the Serbian Radical Party is identical to that of the party founded by Nikola Pasic in 1881.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Is it in fact?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The preamble of the two programmes were indeed identical. In the preamble mention is made of the objective of unifying the Serb people at the time. However, in view of the political reality of Serbia at the end of the 19th century and Serbia at the beginning of the '90s, it cannot be identical because the demands made by the Radicals in 1991 cannot be the same as those of the Radicals in 1881.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I would say that the programme drafted on the basis of the People's Radical Party of 1881, the essential elements are to analyse the Serbian Radical Party one would need other documents there -- which are -- and I think there are -- such as the declaration of the Radical Party is more important, which takes up much of the programme of the Serb Chetnik Movement.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Well, let's turn to part CXI that begins, "Manifesto of the Serbian Radical Party." It's several pages further in the text you have in front of you. Looking at this manifesto, how does the manifesto of the Serbian Radical Party compare to that of the Serbian Chetnik Movement?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of this statement it is asserted that the Serbian Radical Party, true to the tradition of Radicals or the Radical Movement founded by Nikola Pasic, and then the programme itself, it is very similar to that of the Serbian Chetnik Movement. There were some points that were added to correspond to the political realities of the times.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Looking at paragraph 1 of the manifesto, does it articulate the unification of Serbian lands?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first article, in fact, is identical to the article of the Serbian Chetnik Movement. It mentions the same territories that were indicated previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I note that the monarchy is referred to under point 3. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Points 2 and 3 were added in the programme of the Serbian Radical Party, and these are two new points in relation to the Chetnik Movement, because the Chetnik Movement was not -- was devoted to the monarchy, and this was not fully taken into account. And an important point is the point regarding the referendum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Moving on from this question very quickly. The question of the monarchy, in my view, appears to have been taken into consideration by the Serbian Radical Party. It is indicated in its programme.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The monarchist tradition is taken into consideration, but they say that a referendum needs to be organised, and this is what happens in most countries which decide to take such a step. But at the time, Vojislav Seselj was far less inclined towards the restoration of the monarchy because he didn't trust Aleksandar Karadjordjevic who, according to him, had a tendency to put on the same footing the Ustashas and the Chetniks during the Second World War. So he didn't see him as somebody who would sufficiently defend the Serbian national cause. He saw him to be too liberal and who wouldn't give sufficient support to this movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but within this Serbian Radical Party, Dr. Seselj, was he the alpha and omega of the party or were there other persons who could say we want this question of the monarchy to be included in the programme. And as he was not, perhaps, the alpha and omega he would have accepted this being included in the text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there were criticisms that were taken into consideration, criticisms even among former Chetnik fighters in the United States. They felt that he wasn't sufficiently defending the monarchy and the royal Karadjordjevic family and these elements were taken into consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who were the other families, Obrenovic and Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Obrenovic was one of the dynasties ruling in Serbia in the 19th century but after the assassination of the King in 1903, the Karadjordjevics took over and it is the Karadjordjevics who have claims on the throne. The Petrovics are the royal family of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague is telling me that it is time for the break. We will now have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we mark this with a P number before we leave so we can clean up that last detail.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, MFI P153.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell me, please, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- could you please let me know whether I will be able to start my cross-examination today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. First we need to have the number clearly indicated on the transcript. Could the registrar please repeat it. Give us the number once again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, MFI P153.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Dahl, you have one hour seven minutes left, so when we resume, this means that Mr. Seselj will not be able to begin before tomorrow. So we meet again in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The hearing's resumed. I'm going to give you the floor in a moment, Ms. Dahl. Could you finish it all by 1.15? That would be great. I'll make an effort not to ask any more questions myself so that you can use this full hour and the seven minutes left to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I will endeavour to do that, but I wanted to reiterate that I welcome the Bench's questions and wish to satisfy every curiosity you may have about the case and the evidence that supports it. Two brief matters regarding the conduct of the case. Further to your instruction to indicate to Dr. Seselj whether or not there were areas on which the parties could agree and eliminate the necessity for the presentation of evidence, I sent a letter to Dr. Seselj on 3rd of January with an invitation to meet and a list of proposed agreed facts. I also on 7 December 2007 sent a list of documents authored by or uttered by Dr. Seselj with an indication that I would like his position of whether he objected or agreed to their admission into evidence. I am preparing the written motion and would like to be able to state his position. To date I have received no response to either of these letters and would like to avail myself of the good offices of the Chamber to have an exchange of information with Dr. Seselj on these two topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, very briefly. You know that I had invited both parties to come together to try and agree on specific items to save time. Ms. Dahl said that she sent a letter on the 7th of December to you and she has not yet had an answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you issued an order as the Pre-Trial Judge in mid-October, as far as I can remember. So that was 20 days -- over 20 days before the beginning of the trial. I was waiting for Ms. Dahl to contact me. She didn't do so. The trial started on 7th of November. Ms. Dahl's letter and the suggestion -- together with the suggestion of the facts she thought weren't in dispute I received on the 3rd or the 4th of January. So that was two and a half months after you issued your order. So I now have the right to wait for two and a half months before I respond to Ms. Dahl. Naturally I'm joking to a certain extent. Don't hold this against me. The case started on the 7th of November. Ms. Dahl and I are now in the arena and now only one of us can be knocked out in the arena. There's nothing that has to be agreed on. She had her opportunity, as did her predecessors. That was the case for four or five years almost. Much could have been agreed on. She, too, could have given up on many accusations in the indictment and that would have been possible had she examined many of the documents I had. This would have saved the Prosecution and the Court much time, but the Prosecution didn't want to proceed in this way, although I kept the door open for her for four years. But since nothing was done I believe that that concludes the matter. We're now in the ring and we should now see the arguments each party has to present. She's going to be in a more difficult position now because she wasn't in a position to check up certain things by confronting me directly but it's not my fault. So I don't know what we could now discuss given that the trial has already commenced. And secondly, I don't have time for discussions of any kind. I am now involved in preparing for each and every day of the case, so I don't know what there is to discuss.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly. Well, it so happens that you wear two hats. You are an accused, but you are your own lawyer. So you are also a Defence counsel. In trials before this Tribunal, Defence counsel meet with the Prosecution in corridors. They discuss. They try to agree on specific points. This was my concern. I wanted a dialogue to take place. Of course each party is free to maintain their position, but sometimes you can have a fruitful dialogue. There can be good surprises at the end of it. Indeed at the time when I launched the idea, you had said nothing against the idea of a meeting, and then the Prosecution took some time. I was surprised by that, because I'd asked them what they were doing, and I hadn't had an answer at the time. Apparently now the response came on the 7th of December. So you've received a letter. It's up to you now. My only part in this is to facilitate the contacts between the two parties. If there cannot be any dialogue, well, so be it. At least I would have done my level best. This is what I wanted to say in this respect. Yes, Ms. Dahl?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I understand Dr. Seselj's position to be that he is no longer willing to meet on the question of exhibits to be tendered that were authored or uttered by him. I presented a list and I would be grateful if he would indicate whether he has an objection to their admission, and if so, the nature of the objection so that we may attempt to resolve them. That is something that he can do entirely in writing and I would welcome his annotation on the list itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj. There's a host of documents concerning you that you authored. If there is no objection, just say so, and this way Ms. Dahl can at some point ask the documents to be admitted. She'll name all the exhibits saying that she got your approval on them. It's just as simple as that, especially because there are many documents from the Serbian Radical Party or written by you. So let's try to save time. Yes, in this respect do you have anything to say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, first of all I'd like to correct something. We're not talking about the 7th of December but about the 3rd of January. That is the date of Ms. Dahl's letter addressed to myself. So it's over two and a half months from the time you issued your instruction. As far as these documents are concerned, Ms. Dahl sent me the documents before the expert witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl is on her feet. If I understand well, she sent you a letter on the 7th of December, but you got the translation only on the 3rd of January. Is that so, Ms. Dahl?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Two letters, two topics. December 7, exhibits; January 3rd, the meeting on agreed facts. Both were presented to him in a language that he can understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there were two letters, one on the points of agreement and the other on documents, exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we have now dealt with that suggestion on agreed facts. Nothing has been agreed on, so everything is in dispute. So I would now just focus on this second issue. Prior to hearing the witness Oberschall on the 7th or 8th of December, I received five binders, as far as I can remember, in which there were documents and I received a cover letter from Ms. Dahl in which she informed me that after the hearing of the witness Oberschall, which was to cover Tuesday and Wednesday, after this hearing on Thursday she was going to suggest that the documents be admitted into evidence. I immediately answered her letter and asked for a binder of those documents in the Serbian language because I had that list in English alone. She subsequently sent me the documents in the Serbian language. I brought all the documents into the courtroom with me. You saw the guards carrying four large boxes into the courtroom, I think. However, there was no time. After the hearing of the expert witness Oberschall, you put an end to the hearing. I don't think a single document can be tendered into evidence if it is not in accordance with the Rules, if there is no discussion. Each document has been identified here in the courtroom and it is then admitted into evidence, which means that I have the right here in the courtroom to express my position with regard to each and every document. I examined the documents, and I could agree to having two-thirds of the documents being admitted into evidence because we are dealing with photocopies and translations of my books, but there is more or less a third of the documents whose admission into evidence I would oppose. Each of these documents should at least be mentioned in the courtroom. We can't have them admitted into evidence as a block without respecting the Rules. We should go through each document, and if there's nothing to contest I'd say I agree to this. If there are any objections, I would tell you why I object to having a document admitted into evidence. I think this would be simplest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl, how about this as a solution: You could reorganise the list of documents, those that are not challenged, those of the Serbian Radical Party, those of Mr. Seselj, for instance, and in that list you would give the names of witnesses that will come to testify and to whom the documents will be submitted. In this way, Mr. Seselj will have the list with the witnesses and the documents, and we'll know that this or that document will be submitted and he can express himself. For all the documents that he agrees to, they can have final numbers, but of course you will have to submit them to the witnesses and as part of his cross-examination he could also introduce them. Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must just say the following before Ms. Dahl takes the floor. We're not discussing documents that the testimony of certain or individual witnesses refer to. We're talking about documents that are admitted into evidence without witnesses giving testimony. That's how I understand the matter. So most of the documents aren't documents I would contest but I have to express my position on each document and the name of each document has to be referred to, mentioned here in the courtroom, but you should tell me when we would be doing this so I can bring the full set of the documents. It's not necessary for Ms. Dahl to send me the list again. I have the list in the Serbian language. So you can just specify a date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj. We have a lot of documents, documents that shouldn't be contested because you yourself drafted the documents, but what you are requesting is the possibility of asking questions on the basis of these documents. That's fine and that is why I'm saying that Ms. Dahl should just compile a list of the documents and for each document she should mention the name of the witness who will be appearing and then you will have a method of controlling everything. That's what I wanted to say. And this would enable us to save time. We would be able to give the documents numbers. The documents would be admitted unless there are false, inauthentic documents that you might contest. But that's for you to do. Ms. Dahl, try to carry out the operation once more, compile a new list, mark the witnesses who will come for certain documents, send it to the accused. We'll wait for reply and that will enable us to save time because each time we have a document the registrar has to stand up and give it a number, et cetera. We could have just one operation. So if we have now covered that matter, we can call the witness into the courtroom so that we can continue. Please call the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: In the meantime, Your Honour, my intention was to have us work as professionals, to have Dr. Seselj indicate what of the various own statements of his own he does not contest. I don't believe that there is any question regarding authenticity or relevance, and I'll be happy to try to match the documents with particular witnesses, but in the first instance it would be helpful if he can simply identify those to which he does have some objection to their admission or which would be able to be tendered by his consent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But to do so he needs the full list, the names of the witnesses, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that a problem appears here when we try to see how we could proceed. I think that Ms. Dahl wants me to express my position in writing, and I want to express my position orally in the courtroom. I want to have each document in my hands and say I agree with this, I agree with this, I agree with this, I don't agree with this one because of the following reasons. That's why we disagree. Such an important matter shouldn't be left to an exchange of correspondence. This has to be done here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if necessary this can be done in the courtroom. You'll have the list and on a given day I'll give you the floor and you'll say document X -- I agree with document X, I don't agree with document Y, et cetera, et cetera. And if you say that you agree with a certain document, we'll ask the registrar to give that document a number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I need is to be informed a day in advance that we'll be dealing with the matter on a given day and then I can bring the documents with me to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but you will have a list. You should be provided with a list of the documents. You'll have a column for the witnesses. If necessary, you'll have reference to the relevant paragraph in the indictment, and if you agree, you'll say, For number 1, I agree; number 2, I agree; number 3, I don't agree, et cetera, et cetera. So that's how we'll proceed. Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, let me ask you to return to the statute of the Serbian Radical Party that we were discussing prior to the break. If you continue forward in the reprint, you will see it under CXIII. Can you describe for me the purpose of a political party statute such as this?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the statute defines the internal organisation of a party from its base to the peak. It refers to the party's direction, the direction the party will be following. It refers to the body that will be leading the party and right up to the local committees of the Serbian Radical Party. So it concerns the internal organisation. This document concerns the internal organisation of the party.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did the Serbian Radical Party set up related branches outside of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, there were branches of the Serbian Radical Party in Croatia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and as of '93, 1993, there were such branches in Montenegro, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Was that statute registered by the authorities in Serbia in 1991?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statute of the Serbian Radical Party, yes, but I think that each branch had to register with the local authorities because we had the Serbian Radical Party of the Krajina Republika Srpska and then the Serbian Radical Party of the Republika Srpska. So each branch had to register with the authorities in the local regions in question.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did Dr. Seselj articulate the programme of the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question when you say articulate the -- the programme.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Was there a programme that defined the objectives of the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the declaration that we referred to a while ago. Apart from the official programme they referred to the Radical Party of 1881.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What were the objectives of the Radical Party as it constituted itself in 1991?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, more or less the same objectives as those that had been established by the Serbian Chetnik Movement, because many of the elements of the programme had been taken over without amendment of any kind from the Serbian Radical Party. So the idea was to establish a Greater Serbia which would include all the elements that we have already discussed, would include a state of a rule of law, market economy. There were similar ideas about finding a solution to the Kosovo question. There was certain additions, nevertheless, in relation to this issue. For example, one of the additions was that they suggested that have in the Kosovo region, in the region of Kosovo and Metohija, all the military academies and all the police academies. They were to be located in that region so that the tens of thousands officers and non-commissioned officers and policemen and family members could settle down in the Kosovo area. So this was an idea that was referred to when Mr. Seselj went to the USA and when he held his conferences there in order to introduce his political programme. This was mentioned already in 18 -- in 1989. It wasn't in the Chetnik programme of June 1990. This is important because we can see that it was matter of reinforcing the Serbian population of Kosovo by establishing administrative bodies or institutions there. It was a way of modifying the ethnic structure of the population of Kosovo. Similarly, he encouraged settlement in Kosovo by mentioning higher salaries for those who would find employment in that region.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What became of the Serbian Chetnik Movement upon the creation of the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian Chetnik Movement wasn't disbanded when the Serbian Radical Party was established in February in 1991. It became a section of the Serbian Radical Party as well as the organisations that collectively belonged to the Serbian Chetnik Movement. In particular I have in mind the Serbian Cultural Club. But this section that became part of the Serbian Radical Party is not defined in the statute of the party, at least not in the published versions.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What does it mean to have collective memberships within the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for example, the Serbian Cultural Club which was refounded in September 1990, two days after its foundation it decided to join the Serbian Chetnik Movement as an organisation, as a collective. So that means all the members of the club became members of the Chetnik Movement. But the structure itself remained intact. It wasn't disbanded. It was a collective way of joining this body. Further, Serbian Cultural Club was a section of the Serbian Chetnik Movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This collective membership, was it just a way for the individuals to join this association or was it in fact a matter of individual membership but also a matter of the entity becoming a member?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the members of this organisation decided to join this body. They decided that their organisation should join the Serbian Chetnik Movement. So when the Serbian Radical Party was established, these organisations were maintained, but they became sections of the Serbian Radical Party. So the sections which involved with each other but if you have a look at the founding congress of the Serbian Radical Party you might think that it's the first congress of this political organisation, but in the way in which it was presented by the radicals, it was, in fact, the second congress of the movement because the founding congress should be taken into consideration. So this shows that there was a political continuity of Vojislav Seselj. The history of the Radical Serbian Party is the history of Vojislav Seselj's movement through the Chetnik Movement established in 1990. There is continuity of the programme. What also seems important me with regard to the additions to the programme of the Serbian Radical Party is the following: Item 8, which concerns settling members of Serbian ethnic minorities from neighbouring states in Serbia, for example, from Hungary, Bulgaria and Greece. There's also an item that concerns settling Serbians who live west of the Karlobag-Ogulin-Virovitica line. This line is in the programme of the Serbian Radical Party and this ties up with what I said earlier on. They wanted -- they had the will to settle Serbs who lived to the west of this line in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me ask you to look at the document --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me ask you to look at the document that appears at tab 262. This is an interview with Dr. Seselj published in Revija 92, which he then reprinted in his book entitled "Destruction of the Serbian national being," and I believe the interview date was 31 May 1991. Now, in your report you discuss how Dr. Seselj organised -- I'm sorry, how the Serbian Radical Party organised volunteers when armed incidents broke out in Croatia. Looking at this interview can you summarise what Dr. Seselj about his volunteers?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I heard the correct number of the exhibit. 262 or 162?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: 262. Can you explain how Dr. Seselj -- I'm sorry, can you summarise how Dr. Seselj explained his Chetnik detachments and how they were being deployed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document is 262, madam, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting you, but I'm trying -- I'm looking for item 8 the witness referred to. Page 82, line 14. And I can't find it and it's quite important in my opinion. I would like to see that item. Could one give me the precise references? It was the previous document, but I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: That would be 65 ter Exhibit number 144.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the page, please, because I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: For the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: That is paragraph 8 that -- for the record, that appears within the manifesto of the Serbian Radical Party. May I proceed, Judge Lattanzi?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Okay. Let's turn back to the interview with the journalist. Can you look at the end of the document and indicate who the journalist -- where this interview was being conducted?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Revija 92. The author is Dusan Milovanovic; is that right? 31st of May, 1991. The 31st of May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Now, the journalist asked Dr. Seselj how the volunteers were organised and on which principle they were acting. Can you summarise Dr. Seselj's position on forming units that went into Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say something that I said in my report, but I didn't study the military aspect of the organisation of the Serbian Chetnik Movement. That interested me a little less than the subject that I was working on, but there was a link between the Ravna Gora Serbian Chetnik Movement in the US and Serbian Chetnik volunteers who were sent to Croatia. It was interesting to point out when there was the conflict in Borovo Selo at the beginning of May 1991, after the incident the Vojvoda Momcilo Djujic decorated some of the fighters. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: How did Dr. Seselj describe himself with respect to those fighters?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the military leader. He was a Vojvoda. He was the Vojvoda in the homeland as he had been described at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These decorations - that makes one thing of chocolate medals - these decorations the party provides, it had no legal status. The party would decorate them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the Chetnik Movement that decorated them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As would be the case with any other kind of association that awarded members of the association by giving them a certificate, a medal or something else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were given ranks, not just decorations. One could have been nominated or appointed as a Vojvoda or Major. There was a rank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a rank.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there was a rank. In this case Mr. Todosijevic who participated in the fighting in May 1991, was given the rank of Major, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All these volunteers who were admitted to the army, well, did their military leaders maintain these ranks when this took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't studied the military aspect of the Serbian Chetnik Movement. I kept to the ideology of the political programme, but later in Croatia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina Vojvodas or military leaders were nominated within the movement itself or at least inside the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But my colleague's question was more precise. She wanted to know whether the ranks conferred by the Serbian Radical Party had an effect of any kind on the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, because they were, it seems, under the JNA, but could they have been majors, et cetera, but simple soldiers in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were parallel structures in the JNA. They were supposed to become part of the global military operations. They acted as a form of support. They supported operations, but that didn't mean they didn't have their own parallel organisations, organisations parallel to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What allows you to say that they had a parallel organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, since Momcilo Djujic, the Vojvoda, first conferred ranks and gave decorations, we're dealing with a framework that has nothing to do with the JNA. It was the Chetnik Movement for the emigration in this case, but as soon as there are policies pursued by Momcilo Djujic and Vojislav Seselj, well, Momcilo Djujic no longer continued to confer such ranks. This was done within the Serbian Radical Party and the Serbian Chetnik Movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question put to you by my colleague is somewhat different. We want to know whether the fact that these ranks were conferred by the Serbian Radical Party on certain individuals had an effect of any kind on the JNA, on the Yugoslav People's Army. Did it have an effect of any kind or did it have no effect whatsoever? Perhaps it's a technical question and in that case you can just say, I can't answer the question but perhaps you can; but if you can, try and provide us with additional information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't provide you with a precise answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may aid you, if that means anything. We're dealing with events before the 1st of August, 1991. That was before the JNA had become involved in an armed conflict with Croatian paramilitary formations. Vojvoda Djujic sent a letter in May, and as a sign of recognition he conferred ranks on some individuals. The JNA entered the war on the 1st of August. That was when our volunteers went to serve in the JNA or, rather, when our volunteers went to serve in the JNA as volunteers this was no longer an issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've heard what Mr. Seselj has said. Dr. Seselj says that the ranks conferred upon these individuals were conferred upon them before they had become part of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, at the beginning but our question is later on. You can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I have said I didn't deal with specifically military questions. I was concerned more with political questions and with the Serbian national ideology; so I didn't look into this aspect in detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And the Serbian text on page 226, can you read out the first full paragraph where Dr. Seselj says what he did with volunteers of the Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me some very delicate questions. In any event, it is possible for our Chetniks to be in good form and to check out their military knowledge everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm seeing that you have gone lower on the page. I'm referring to Dr. Seselj's statement that he formed the units on the spot, finishing with his statement that he is their Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found the paragraph now. "We formed the units on the spot. Detachments or other units were formed where the Chetniks needed to act and where we were requested to do so. We did not go anywhere against the will of the Serbian population. We also have detachments of volunteers in various areas of Serbian Krajina, Western Srem and Baranja. We either sent them from here, from this reduced Serbia, or from the Chetnik organisation in the field, from among the Serbs who live there. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, for example, there was no need to send the Chetniks from Serbia. We have a Chetnik command in Romanija, a strong Chetnik movement in North-eastern Bosnia, and in Eastern Herzegovina. We, of course, have the Supreme Command, and I am the Supreme Commander."

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: How do you interpret Dr. Seselj's statements about the military activities of his political party?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can see that -- that various units were formed consisting either of persons living in the region, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, for example, or by forming units of Serbian volunteers in Serbia proper.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: May I have a P number for 65 ter Exhibit 262?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number P154.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Would you consider this combination of Dr. Seselj's political and ideological and apparent military leadership typical for a Chetnik commander?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I haven't understood your question very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Historically, did Chetnik commanders exercise a trilogy of leadership, that is political, ideological, as well as military leadership?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular case, yes. We are in a rather ambiguous situation. A political formation leads -- fits into a military tradition so that the party acts on two fronts. It is not a question of a simple political party. It has a pronounced military dimension as well that has to be taken into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: In your report you summarised some of Dr. Seselj's political proposals during the war concerning exchange of population. Can you briefly summarise the views that you found in researching his political positions?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are various occasions in interviews with the press in 1991 and 1992 when reference is made to population exchanges between Croats and Serbs, Croats and Serbia and Serbs in Croatia. For example, in 1991, Vojislav Seselj declared that a hundred thousand Croats should leave Serbia so that Serb refugees from Croatia can be settled there. These positions were repeated in 1992, including in the National Assembly of Serbia on the 1st of April, 1992, when exchange of populations was presented as a positive measure. And in his speech, he declared, "We're going to expel Croats from Serbia."

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What happened after Dr. Seselj advocated that solution for the Croats in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This proposition, this measure, considered the Croats of Vojvodina principally, because that is where they are most numerous. And also in the region of Srem there was some tension in the spring of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Would you reproduce Seselj's speech in the National Assembly of Serbia on the 1st of April 1992 in your report?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is stated he declared --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 89, line 24, the witness spoke of measures of reprisal, not positive measures. Measures of reprisal. I am not very familiar with the English language, but I don't think that the translation was correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said they were measures of reprisal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were presented as such by Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Would you read -- would you please read into the record the excerpt of Dr. Seselj's speech to the National Assembly of Serbia on 1st of April, 1992, that you have placed in your report.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "One other thing. If the Croats are expelling the Serbs in such huge numbers from their homes, what are the Croats here in Belgrade waiting for and those throughout Serbia? An exchange of populations just as Tudjman has chased the Serbs from Zagreb, we will expel from Belgrade the same number of Croats. When a Serbian family from Zagreb arrives, they will live in the home of Croats from Belgrade in return for the keys to their home in Zagreb, an exchange."

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Was this understood to be a voluntary or an enforced exchange of populations? And we're referring now to page 89 of your report in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the terms used, it -- one could say that it was more of a forced exchange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is something that attracts my attention. In his speech, he speaks of keys, the keys to the home in Zagreb, an exchange. So there is an exchange of keys. A family A will take the apartment of family B, and family B will take the apartment of family A. So there is an exchange of keys. And this exchange, according to what I read, is not being done with the help of a soldier with a rifle behind each individual. According to what the sentence says, family A which comes from Zagreb to Belgrade, for example, takes the keys of an apartment in Belgrade and hands over the keys of their apartment in Zagreb to the Croat family which leaves Belgrade to go to Zagreb. If the words have any meaning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says as many Croats that we will expel from Belgrade, which means that the Croats of Belgrade have no choice. They will be forced to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is stated in the Serbian language? Is it the word "chase out" that is used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Isterati" or "expel," perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you say that the word "chased" means that there was forced, that the expulsion was forced.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It doesn't appear to be a peaceful process. During the census in 2002, 8.000 Croats are living in Belgrade, mostly mixed couples. Would these people have had a choice? I really don't know. I don't think any -- these people had any choice. It was imposed upon them.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did Dr. Seselj maintain cooperative or otherwise relations with political parties in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina during the war?
